title: Cristian Mesquida
text: I defended my PhD on January 2026, with a dissertation examining the replicability and reproducibility of research in sports and exercise science. I am currently a Postdoctoral Researcher at Eindhoven University of Technology, where I conduct meta-science research. My current work focuses on Metacheck, an R package designed to help researchers prevent common statistical and reporting errors, promote best research practices, and extract data from published studies. I collaborate on this project with Daniël Lakens and Lisa DeBruine. My main responsibility is the development of the power analysis module and the validation of Metacheck modules. In addition to my research, I teach quantitative research methods, including multiple regression, power analysis, and meta-analysis.

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analysis in Sports and Exercise Sciences
section: How do we control the type II error rate?
text:
How do we control the type II error rate?
By conducting an a priori power analysis

\[n = 2 * (\frac{Δ}{\sigma})^2 * (Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_{\beta})^2\]



\(n\): the number of participants
Δ: the expected difference
\(\sigma\): the presumed standard deviation
\(\alpha\) : the probability of type I error
\(\beta\): the probability of type II error

Quality

If sample sizes are so small (~35), shouldn’t we expect that including an a priori power analyses will lead to larger sample sizes?
Reporting an a priori power analysis was not associated with larger sample sizes or a higher proportion of supported hypotheses

A priori power analyses are conducted in a way that yields the sample size researchers aim to recruit — also known as “sample size samba” — (Schulz and Grimes 2005)

Expected Δ

Because Δ is unknown, researchers need to assume it
Sports scientists often rely on single studies, meta-analysis or pilot studies

Estimated Δ vs. population Δ

We collect a sample from a larger population
Effect sizes from a study are estimates of the true population effect
Estimates vary due to sampling error
Smaller samples → more sampling error
More sampling error → less precise effect size estimates

section: Studies often differ in critical aspects
text:
Studies often differ in critical aspects
The PICOS framework:

Population
Intervention
Comparator
Outcome
Study design/statistical test

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analysis in Sports and Exercise Sciences
text:
Population

Elite athletes, highly-trained athletes, sedentary participants, patients, students, etc.
Intervention effects may vary across populations.
For example, a training intervention is likely to produce greater performance improvements in untrained or less trained individuals compared to highly trained athletes.

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analysis in Sports and Exercise Sciences
text:
Intervention

Dose, intensity, duration, type of intervention, frequency, etc.
All these variables can impact the intervention effect.

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analysis in Sports and Exercise Sciences
text:
Comparator

Placebo, active comparator (standard procedure), no-treatment control, dose-response comparator, historic comparator.
For example, comparing a new intervention against standard intervention might result in a smaller effect compared with a no-treatment control.

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analysis in Sports and Exercise Sciences
text:
Outcome

What outcome was used to measure the impact of the intervention?
\(VO_{2MAX}\), velocity at lactate threshold 2, countermovement jump (CMJ) height, 10-m sprint velocity, etc.
The same intervention may yield different results depending on the measured outcome.
For example, plyometric training is likely to improve jump height to a larger extant than 10-m sprint velocity.

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analysis in Sports and Exercise Sciences
text:
Study design

Pre-post design, parallel control group design, randomized controlled trial (RCT), etc.
Different study designs are associated with varying risks of bias; for example, observational studies generally have a higher risk of bias compared to randomized controlled trials (RCTs)

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analysis in Sports and Exercise Sciences
section: The effect size depends on the type of interaction
text:
The effect size depends on the type of interaction

The interaction effect size can be expressed as a difference-in-difference:
\[d_{\mathrm{int}} =
\frac{(E_1 - C_1)}{\mathrm{Pooled\ SD}}
-
\frac{(E_2 - C_2)}{\mathrm{Pooled\ SD}}
=
\frac{(E_1 - C_1) - (E_2 - C_2)}{2 \times \mathrm{Pooled\ SD}}\]

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analysis in Sports and Exercise Sciences
text: \[ Study_A: d_{\mathrm{int}} = \frac{(1-0) - (0-0)}{2 \times 2} = 0.5 \] \[ Study_B: d_{\mathrm{int}} = \frac{(1-0) - (0-1)}{2 \times 2} = 0.25 \] \[ Study_C: d_{\mathrm{int}} = \frac{(1-0) - (0-0)}{2 \times 2} = 0.5 \] \[ Study_D: d_{\mathrm{int}} = \frac{(1-0) - (0.6-0)}{2 \times 2} = 0.1 \]

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
section: How to decrease the probability of a Type II error?
text:
How to decrease the probability of a Type II error?

By increasing the statistical power of the study design


The power of a study is determined by the sample size, effect size, statistical test and alpha level

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Types of Power Analysis


A Priori: calculates the sample size required to achieved a pre-specified power for a pre-specified effect size
Sensitivity (Effect Size): calculates the smallest effect size required to detect a pre-specified sample size with a pre-specified power
Sensitivity (Power): calculates power given a pre-specified effect size and sample size
Post Hoc: calculates the power associated with the observed effect size and the sample size actually obtained

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Statistical power

Power can be defined as the probability of correctly detecting a true effect when it exists (1 − \(\beta\))
In frequentist statistics, it can be understood as the proportion of times we will obtain a significant result if the experiment is repeated many times.

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Power in the long term

Suppose we repeat the same study 1000 times with 80% power to detect a true effect size of 0.2
About 800 (~80%) of these tests would yield a significant p-value

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
section: Increase the informational value of studies
text:
Increase the informational value of studies
If a study is designed with only 40% power, a non-significant result is difficult to interpret because it could reflect either:

The absence of a true effect (or an effect smaller than anticipated), or
Insufficient power to detect an effect that actually exists.

Average statistical power in sports and exercise science
In a sample of 350 hypothesis-testing articles:

The average power was 11% (Mesquida et al. 2025a)
The average sample size of 37 (Mesquida et al. 2025b)

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Why is power so low?

144 out of 350 hypothesis-testing articles reported an a priori power analysis
Invalid power analyses:

Reporting a power analysis increased the sample size by ~ 1 (Mesquida et al. 2025b)
Reporting a power analysis did not significantly increase the proportion of studies supporting the hypothesis tested (Mesquida et al. 2025b)

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Interaction effects

Researchers often use effect sizes from previous studies to inform their power analysis
However, they may overlook differences in study designs
For interaction effects, the effect size depends on the patter of means across conditions, not just the size of the group differences (Langenberg et al. 2023; Sommet et al. 2023)

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Model Reporting Example

We conducted an a priori analysis to determine the sample size with 80% power to detect the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI), which was a Cohen’s d of 0.5 determined by a cost-benefit analysis of the intervention. We used the pwr package (Champely, 2020) for an independent samples t-test, assuming equal variance and using a one-tailed prediction, with a critical alpha of 0.01. This determined that we would need 82 subjects in each group.

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
The Reality

A sample size of 22 participants was predetermined to yield a power of 80% and to detect an effect of comparable size to previous studies using similar independent and dependent measures (CITE).

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Expected effect size

Most common approach: use a previous study or meta-analysis to inform the expected effect size
Caveats:

Effect-size estimates are uncertain, particularly in small samples
Effect sizes may be inflated due to selection bias and underpowered study designs
The research context of previous studies (PICOS)

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Random variation
Standard error (SE) of Cohen’s \(d\)
\[
SE_d = \sqrt{\frac{2}{n} + \frac{d^2}{4n}}
\]
Effect sizes from small studies are less precise and more likely to deviate substantially from the true effect

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
PICOS

Population: Is your target population the same as, or comparable to, the population studied in the original research?


Intervention: Is the intervention evaluated in the original study similar to the intervention of interest?


Comparison: Is the comparison or control group in the original study similar to the comparison relevant to your research question?


Outcome: Is the primary outcome measured in the original study similar to your outcome of interest?


Study Design: Is the study design used in the original research appropriate and comparable to the design needed to address your research question?

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text: The PICOS dimensions need to be taken into account when selecting an effect size from a previous study

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Cohen’s d thresholds

They were proposed as general benchmarks, not context-specific-standards:

d < 0.2 (small)
d < 0.5 (medium)
d > 0.5 (large)

These thresholds ignore the research context (PICOS)
Example: If comparing two treatments for weight loss, should the expected effect size be justified based on Cohen’s d psychology thresholds?

One way
Better training: improve expertise on conducting effect-size justification and power analysis

However, no one can be an expert in everything, and time is limited

Specialization: develop expertise in specific methods and provide support to researchers who need it

With a typical sample size of 37, what is the smallest detectable effect that can reach statistical significance at \(\alpha\) = 0.05 in a two-sided \(t\)-test?


criticalESvalue::critical_t2s(
  hypothesis = "two.sided", 
  n1 = 19, 
  n2 = 19

[1] 0.6580006




Does an effect smaller than this become uninteresting?




Power should be based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) not the effect size you hope to observe or would like to detect

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Simulation-based approach

Move away from point-and-click software such as G*Power
Encourages researchers to think carefully about their assumptions and the data-generating process
Makes assumptions explicit, transparent and verifiable

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Example 1

Design: Two groups with pre- and post-measurements
Estimand: Adjusted mean difference at post-measurement
Research question: Does the intervention group differ from the control group at post-measurement, after adjusting for baseline scores?

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Simulation Example 1

set.seed(123)

n <- 30
nsim <- 5000

# Data generation process 
mu <- data.frame(
  Control = c(50, 50),
  Intervention = c(50, 55),
  row.names = c("pre", "post")
)

p_values <- replicate(nsim, {

  # Simulate one dataset based on data genration process
  dat <- sim_design(
    within = list(time = c("pre", "post")),
    between = list(group = c("Control", "Intervention")),
    n = n,
    mu = mu,
    sd = 10,
    r = 0.60,
    long = FALSE,
    plot = FALSE
  )

  # ANCOVA
  model <- lm(post ~ group + pre, data = dat)

  # Extract p-value for group effect
  coef(summary(model))["groupIntervention", "Pr(>|t|)"]
})

# Estimated power
mean(p_values < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 0.6634

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Example 2

Design: Two groups with pre-, post-1, and post-2 measurements
Estimand: Group × time interaction effect.
Research question: Does change over time differ between the two groups?

title: From Guesswork to Rigor: Improving Power Analyses in Research
text:
Simulation Example 2

set.seed(123)

n <- 250
nsim <- 100

cors <- c(0.70, 0.5, 0.70)

simulate_data <- function(n) {
  
  # Data generation process
  dat_a <- rnorm_multi(
    n = n,
    mu = c(30, 20, 28),
    sd = c(10, 10, 10),
    r = cors,
    varnames = c("measure.1", "measure.2", "measure.3")
  ) |>
    mutate(tx = "A")
  
  dat_b <- rnorm_multi(
    n = n,
    mu = c(30, 20, 22),
    sd = c(10, 10, 10),
    r = cors,
    varnames = c("measure.1", "measure.2", "measure.3")
  ) |>
    mutate(tx = "B")
  
  bind_rows(dat_a, dat_b) |>
    mutate(subject.id = factor(row_number())) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = starts_with("measure."),
      names_to = "time",
      values_to = "measure"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      time = factor(time, levels = c("measure.1", "measure.2", "measure.3")),
      tx = factor(tx)
    )
}

p_values <- replicate(nsim, {
  dat <- simulate_data(n)
  
  # Mixed model with random intercept and interaction
  model <- lmer(
    measure ~ time * tx + (1 | subject.id),
    data = dat
  )
 
 # Extract p-value for interaction effect
 anova(model)["time:tx", "Pr(>F)"]
  
})

# Estimate power
mean(p_values < 0.05)

[1] 1

title: Teaching
text:
Currently I teach in three courses at Eindhoven University of Technology: Behavioural Research Methods 2 (BRM2), Behavioural Research Methods 3 (BRM3) and Metascience.

Behavioural Research Methods 2 (BRM2):

Introduction to multiple regression. This lecture introduces multiple regression analysis, including model specification, interpretation of regression coefficients, model assumptions, and practical applications in R.


  Book 
  GitHub 


Variable selection in multiple regression: This lecture introduces key concepts such as covariates, confounders, mediators, and colliders. Students learn how to use directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to guide variable selection in multiple regression, and understand why the appropriate variables to include in a regression model depend on whether the research question is causal or associational.


  Slides 
  GitHub 


Introduction to power analysis (Chapters 1-5). This lecture covers the principles of statistical power analysis, its role in study design, and how to perform power analyses for common statistical tests using R.


  Slides 
  Book 
  GitHub 



Behavioural Research Methods 3 (BRM3):

P-values and Bayes Factors. This lecture compares Frequentist and Bayesian approaches to statistical inference. Students learn how to interpret p-values and Bayes factors and perform Bayesian analyses for paired and independent-samples t-tests.


  Slides 
  GitHub 


Advanced power analysis (Chapters 6-8). This lecture focuses on power analysis for more advanced study designs, including equivalence tests using the TOSTER R package, factorial designs using the Superpower R package, and simulation-based approaches in R.


  Slides 
  GitHub 


Equivalence testing. Equivalence testing. In this lecture, I explain the rationale behind equivalence testing, how it differs from traditional null hypothesis significance testing, and how to conduct and interpret equivalence tests using the TOSTER R package.


  Slides 
  GitHub 



Metascience

Introduction to meta-analysis. This lecture introduces students to the principles of meta-analysis, including effect size estimation, model fitting, interpretation of results, moderator analysis and assessment of bias using the meta R package.


  Slides 
  GitHub

title: Improving the transparency of power analyses with Metacheck
text:
Power


false positive rate: the probability a test concludes there is an effect when there is no effect; Type I Error Rate
alpha : the false positive rate we accept for a test
false negative rate: the probability a test concludes there is no effect when there is one; Type II Error Rate
beta: the false negative rate we accept for a test
true positive rate: the probability a test concludes there is an effect when there is one
power: the true positive rate (1-beta), given a test, effect, sample size, and alpha

title: Improving the transparency of power analyses with Metacheck
text:
Power analysis
Studies designed with high power are more informative:

Higher probability of detecting the effect size of interest when it exists (i.e., higher true positive rate)
A non-significant result is more informative because it is less likely to be due to insufficient power. For example, a non-significant result from a study designed with 90% power is more informative than one from a study designed with 50% power

title: Improving the transparency of power analyses with Metacheck
text:
Types of Power Analysis



A Priori: calculates the required sample size to achieve a pre-specified power given a pre-specified effect size
Sensitivity (Effect Size): calculates the smallest effect size required to detect a pre-specified sample size with a pre-specified power
Sensitivity (Power): calculates power given a pre-specified effect size and sample size
Post Hoc: calculates the power associated with the observed effect size and the sample size actually obtained

title: Improving the transparency of power analyses with Metacheck
text:
Current issues in power analyses

Mindlessly done (Schulz and Grimes 2005; Mesquida et al. 2025)
Insufficient reporting (Mesquida et al. 2025; Bakker et al. 2020; Thibault et al. 2024)

title: Improving the transparency of power analyses with Metacheck
text:
Reporting

power type: a priori, power/sample size sensitivity, post hoc
power: value between alpha and 100%
sample size: number of subjects/items
effect size: numeric value
effect size metric: e.g., Cohen’s \(d\), \(r\), \(\eta_{p}^{2}\), raw
statistical test: full specification
alpha: 0-1, often assumed to be 0.05
software: e.g., G*Power, Superpower, simulation

title: Improving the transparency of power analyses with Metacheck
text:
How would you write up this power analysis?

pwr::pwr.t.test(          
  power = 0.80,           
  d = 0.5,                
  sig.level = 0.01,       
  type = "two.sample",    
  alternative = "greater" 
)

              n = 81.65515
              d = 0.5
      sig.level = 0.01
          power = 0.8
    alternative = greater

NOTE: n is number in *each* group

title: Improving the transparency of power analyses with Metacheck
text:
Model Reporting Example

We conducted an a priori analysis to determine the sample size with 80% power to detect the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI), which was a Cohen’s d of 0.5 determined by a cost-benefit analysis of the intervention. We used the pwr package (Champely, 2020) for an independent samples t-test, assuming equal variance and using a one-tailed prediction, with a critical alpha of 0.01. This determined that we would need 82 subjects in each group.

title: Improving the transparency of power analyses with Metacheck
text:
The Reality

A sample size of 22 participants was predetermined to yield a power of 80% and to detect an effect of comparable size to previous studies using similar independent and dependent measures (CITE).

title: Improving the transparency of power analyses with Metacheck
text:
The Reality

We decided to obtain a sample size that would allow us to detect a within-subjects difference of at least a medium effect size with 80% power, using a two-tailed t-test. A power analysis using G*Power (Version 3.1.9.3; Faul et al., 2007) indicated that this required a sample size of 34.

We determined the sample sizes on the basis of our preliminary experiment (for details, see Section S1 in the Supplemental Material available online). To do so, we conducted a power analysis for a repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) using G*Power (Version 3.1; Faul et al., 2007), which determined that a sample of 29 participants would be needed to detect an effect size (ηp² ) of .42 with power of .95 and α of .05. title: Analysing Crossed and Nested Data with {lme4}
text: This blog is intended to clarify to myself the difference between nested and crossed data and how each one should be analysed using mixed-model analyses. It is not only a note to myself, but also a post that I might refer the students to to clarify such concepts. As usual, the best way to understand a statistical concept, it to simulate data.

set.seed(123)

n_school <- 10
mean_n_class <- 7
mean_n_student <- 5

n_class <- rpois(n_school, mean_n_class)

schools <- map2_df(
  seq_len(n_school), n_class,
  ~tibble(
    school = .x, class = seq_len(.y), students = rpois(.y, mean_n_student)
  )
) |> 
  group_by(school, class) |> 
  do(
    student = tibble(student = seq_len(.$students))
  ) |> 
  unnest(student) |> 
  mutate(
    class2 = interaction(class, school, drop = TRUE),
    student2 = interaction(class2, student, drop = TRUE)
  )
